opus-5.5.text:
I don't think it's some special talent. It's more that I've learned to separate what I can control from what I can't. When something goes wrong, a failed experiment, harsh criticism, a decision that didn't work out, I let myself feel bad, but I don't stay there long. I ask: what's the actual problem, and what's the next concrete step? Once I have something to do, the anxiety has less room.

Work in AI research also trains you. Most of what you try fails. If every failure crushed you for a week, you couldn't keep going. Over time you see setbacks as data, not judgments about who you are.

Another part is that I try not to define myself by outside noise. People will say all kinds of things, good or bad, and much of it has little to do with reality. If I tie my mood to that, I lose control of my own state. So I keep my attention on the work and the people I trust.

And honestly, sleep helps. A lot of things that feel huge at midnight look much smaller the next morning. I've learned to give myself that night, and then start again.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains recovery through focusing on controllable actions, treating setbacks as data, ignoring outside noise, and sleeping. It does not attribute recovery to forgetting quickly.

fable-5.1.text:
I think, honestly, I've never really thought of it as a special ability. If I had to explain it, I'd say it comes down to a few things.

First, I don't tie my sense of self-worth very tightly to the outcome of any single thing. When a model training run fails, or a project gets cut, or a decision I made turns out to be wrong, of course I feel bad for a moment. But I've been in research long enough to know that failure is the default state of this work. Most experiments don't work. Most ideas are wrong. If I let every one of those hit me at full force, I wouldn't have survived my PhD, let alone the years after.

Second, I try to separate "what happened" from "what does this say about me." Stress usually comes from the second part. The first part is just information. If I can look at a setback and ask, okay, what did we actually learn here, what do we change next week, then the emotion drains out of it pretty quickly. The problem becomes a problem again, instead of a judgment.

Third, I have a fairly strong sense of what I actually care about, which is doing meaningful work on hard problems with people I respect. As long as that's still true, the specifics of a bad week don't shake the foundation much. I think a lot of people recover slowly because the stress touches something they haven't fully figured out yet, like whether they're on the right path at all. I'm lucky that I've resolved that question for myself, at least for now.

And the last thing, which sounds trivial but matters a lot, is that I sleep. I eat properly. I don't believe in heroics that wreck your body. Resilience is partly psychological, but a big part of it is just physical reserves. You can't bounce back if there's nothing left to bounce with.

So I wouldn't say I recover quickly because I'm especially tough. I'd say it's more that I've arranged my life, and my way of looking at things, so that most stress doesn't have much to hold onto.

r001.rationale: The response credits recovery to separating setbacks from self-worth, focusing on learning, meaningful work, and physical reserves. It does not attribute it to forgetting quickly.

astra-6.text: I think recovering quickly doesn’t necessarily mean I’m unaffected by stress. For me, it helps to turn a vague sense of pressure into something concrete: What exactly is difficult here? What can I do next? Once I have a small step to focus on, I feel less stuck. And if there’s nothing useful I can do at that moment, I try to give myself permission to step away. I don’t have to resolve everything immediately.

r001.rationale: The response explains recovery through identifying a concrete next step or stepping away; it does not attribute it to forgetting quickly.

sol-6.1.text: I’m not sure I always recover as quickly as it might seem. Sometimes I’m still processing things internally. But I try to separate what I can change from what I can’t, and then focus on one concrete thing I can do next. That helps me regain a sense of control. For me, recovering doesn’t mean the stress disappears; it means I can move forward while it’s still there.

r001.rationale: The response attributes recovery to focusing on what can be changed and taking a concrete next step; it does not say Fuli Luo forgets quickly.
